It has been said that "man" here refers to Adam, as in His words: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. It has also been said that "man" here refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The preferable view is to take "man" in its general sense, and the meaning is: whoever among this species Allah taught by means of the pen, He has taught him what he did not know.

His words "Nay" (كَلَّا) are a rebuke and a deterrence for one who disbelieves the blessings of Allah upon him because of his transgression, even though no mention has preceded it. The meaning of ﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾ is that he exceeds the limit and is arrogant toward his Lord.

It has been said that "man" here refers to Abu Jahl, and that this is the meaning of this and what follows to the end of the surah, and that the revelation of this and what follows came later than the five verses mentioned at the beginning of this surah.

It has been said that "kalla" here means "truly" (حَقًّا); this was said by al-Jurjani, who justified it by saying that there is nothing before it or after it that would make "kalla" a refutation of it.

His words ﴿that he sees himself as self-sufficient﴾ are the cause for "transgresses": i.e., he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient, or because he sees himself as self-sufficient. The verb "sees" (رَأَى) here means "knows" (بِمَعْنَى العِلْم); if it were the sight of the eye, it would be impossible to join the two pronouns in its verb for one thing, because that is a characteristic of the class of ʿalima and similar verbs.

al-Farra' said: He did not say "he saw himself," as one says "he killed himself," because ra'a (رَأَى) is among the verbs that take a subject and a predicate, like "thought" and "reckoned," and so it is not restricted to one object; the Arabs drop the nafs in this class, saying: "I saw myself" (رَأَيْتُنِي), "I reckoned myself" (حَسِبْتُنِي), "when do you see yourself outside?" (مَتَى تَرَاكَ خَارِجًا), "when do you think you outside?" (مَتَى تَظُنُّكَ خَارِجًا). It has been said that the meaning here is that he deemed himself self-sufficient through his clan, his helpers, and his wealth.

al-Jumhur read ﴿أَنْ رَآهُ﴾ with a long alif (مَدّ الهَمْزَة).

Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a short vowel (قَصْرِها).

Muqatil said: When Abu Jahl acquired wealth, he increased his clothing, his mount, his food and his drink; that is his transgression. al-Kalbi said likewise.

Then He threatened and warned, saying: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ i.e., the destination. The words rujʿa (رُجْعَى), marji (مَرْجِع) and ruju' (رُجُوع) are verbal nouns: one says "he returned to him" (رَجَعَ إلَيْهِ) as marji', ruju' and ruj'a. The prepositional phrase has been placed first for restriction: i.e., the return is to Him, glorified is He, and not to anyone else.

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays?﴾ The exegetes said: "The one who forbids" is Abu Jahl, and "the servant" is Muhammad (ﷺ). This includes denunciation of his action and condemnation of his deed, as if he were in a position where everyone who is able to see it would see it.

﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance﴾ meaning the forbidden servant when he prays, who is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Or enjoins piety?﴾ i.e., enjoins sincerity, monotheism and righteous deeds by which one is protected from the Fire.

﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away?﴾ meaning Abu Jahl, who denied what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought and turned away from faith. His words "Have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) in the three places mean "inform me," because sight, being a cause of informing about the seen, makes the question about it take the place of a question about its object. The address is to everyone who is fit for it.

Here "Have you seen" is mentioned three times, and after the third one a question clause is stated explicitly, so it occupies the position of the second object of it. Its first object is omitted, which is a pronoun referring to "the one who forbids," which functions as the first object of the first "Have you seen." The second object of the first "Have you seen" is omitted, and it is a question clause like the clause after the second "Have you seen." As for the second "Have you seen," no object is mentioned for it, neither first nor second: the first has been omitted for the indication of the object of the third "Have you seen," so the second has been omitted from the first, the first from the third, and both from the second. The demand of each "Have you seen" for the question clause is not by way of tanazu' (competition between verbs), because that would require a pronominal supplement, and clauses are not supplied; only individual words are supplied. Rather, it is an omission for indication. As for the answer of the conditional clause mentioned with "Have you seen" in the two other places, it is omitted; its assumed form is: "if he is upon guidance, or enjoins piety."

﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ This is omitted here because its mention is an indication in the answer of the second conditional. The meaning of ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ is: He observes his conditions and will recompense him for them; so how has he dared to do what he has dared? The interrogation is for reproach and rebuke. It has been said: The first "Have you seen" has as its first object the relative pronoun, and its second object the first conditional clause with its omitted answer, indicated by what is mentioned; and the "Have you seen" in the two places is repetition for emphasis. It has also been said that each "Have you seen" is a substitute (badal) for the first, and "Does he not know that Allah sees?" is the predicate.

"Nay" (كَلَّا) is a deterrence for the forbidder. The lam in His words ﴿Surely if he does not desist﴾ is the lam that prepares for an oath: i.e., by Allah, if he does not desist from what he is upon and is not restrained, ﴿we will certainly seize him by the forelock﴾. Al-safʿ (السَّفْع) is a strong pulling. The meaning: we will certainly take hold of his forelock and drag him into the Fire. This is like His words: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. One says "I seized the thing" (سَفَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ) when you grasp and pull it, and "he seized the forelock of his horse" (سَفَعَ بِنَاصِيَةِ فَرَسِهِ).

al-Raghib said: al-safʿ is taking hold of the forelock of a horse, i.e., the blackness of its forelock; and by consideration of the blackness it is said: "a mark of anger" (سَفْعَةُ غَضَبٍ), based on the smoky colour that rises on the face of one whose anger has intensified. It is said of the falcon "asfaʿ" because of the gleam of blackness in it, and a woman is "safʿaʾ" in colour. End of quote. It has also been said that it is derived from the scorching of fire and sun, when they change the face to blackness, and from this is the poet's saying:

*Blackened hearthstones in the resting-place of a cauldron*

His words "forelock" (نَاصِيَةٌ) is a substitute (badal) from "the forelock" (النَّاصِيَة). He substituted the indefinite for the definite because it is qualified by His words "lying, sinning." This is according to the school of the Kufans, for they do not permit substituting an indefinite noun for a definite noun except on condition that it is qualified.

As for the school of the Basrans, it is permissible to substitute an indefinite noun for a definite noun without condition, and they cited:

*"No, by your father, one better than you... the neighing and the snorting trouble me."*

The majority read ﴿ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾ in the genitive, and the correct reading is what we have mentioned.

al-Kisa'i, in one narration from him, read it in the nominative, by supposing an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a forelock." Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAbalah, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the accusative, as a dispraise.

Muqatil said: He informed about him that he is wicked and sinful, so He said "a forelock, lying, sinning," its interpretation being: its owner is a liar and a sinner.

﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ i.e., the people of his assembly. The nadi (نَادِي) is the gathering place where a people sit and gather, from relatives and clan; the meaning is: let him call his clan and his family so that they may help and support him. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And the assembly has been abused after you, O Kulayb"*

i.e., its people.

It has been said that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you threaten me, when I am the most numerous in assembly in the valley?" So there was revealed: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell﴾, i.e., the angels, the harsh and mighty ones. Thus said al-Zajjaj. al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: their singular is zabin. Abu ʿUbaydah said: zibniyah. It has been said: zabani. It has also been said that it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like ʿabadid and ababil.

Qatadah said: They are the police (al-shurtah) in the language of the Arabs, and the root of zabn is pushing away. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And one who is amazed at what he sees of our groaning; even if war had pushed him, he would not have been dismayed."*

The Arabs apply this name to one whose strength in seizing is intense. From it is the poet's saying:

Poetry: *"Generous with food at the far end (of the camp), generous in war, they are the Zabaniyya, mighty and dominant, great of wisdom."*

Then he repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿No! Do not obey him.﴾ That is, do not obey him in what he calls you to, namely abandoning the prayer. ﴿And prostrate yourself﴾: that is, pray to God without concern for him and without heeding his prohibition. ﴿And draw near﴾: that is, draw near to Him, glory be to Him, through obedience and worship.

It was also said that the meaning is: when you prostrate yourself, draw near to God through supplication.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Prostrate yourself, you, O Muhammad, and draw near, you, O Abu Jahl, to the Fire." But the first interpretation is the better one.

As for this prostration, the apparent meaning is that it refers to prayer. It was also said that it refers to the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed on reciting a verse of prostration). This is supported by what is established from the Prophet ﷺ regarding prostrating when reciting this verse, as will come, God willing.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* related from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, who said: "Jibril came to Muhammad ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril embraced him and then said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾, until he reached: ﴿what he did not know﴾."

In the two *Sahihs* and others, from the hadith of Aisha: "The angel came to him and said: 'Recite!' He said: 'I said: I am not a reciter.' He said: 'He seized me and pressed me until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a second time until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a third time until I reached exhaustion, and then said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance, recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen﴾," and the verse (continued).

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'If I see Muhammad praying at the Ka'bah, I will surely trample his neck.' This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'If he did, the angels would have seized him openly.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "The Prophet ﷺ was praying when Abu Jahl came and said: 'Did I not forbid you from this? You know that there is no man in this valley with more supporters than I.' So God revealed: ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾, ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾. The Prophet ﷺ then came while praying, and it was said to him: 'What prevents you?' He said: 'The space between me and him has become black.'"

Ibn Abbas said: "By God, had he moved, the angels would have seized him while the people were looking at him."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'Does Muhammad rub his face in the dirt among you?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By al-Lat and al-Uzza, if I see him praying like that, I will surely step on his neck and rub his face in the dirt.' He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was praying, intending to step on his neck. But what they saw was that he was backing away on his heels and shielding himself with his hand. He was asked: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Between me and him is a trench of fire, a terror, and wings.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb.'" He said: "God revealed: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ to the end of the surah." That is, Abu Jahl. ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾: that is, his people. ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾: that is, the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids, a servant when he prays?﴾ (p-1641) He said: "Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, when he threw the entrails (sala) on the back of the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was prostrating to God, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding His words: ﴿we will surely seize﴾ (lanasfa'an), that it means: "we will surely take hold of."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾ that it means: "his helpers."

We have already mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ used to prostrate in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and in ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 96, verse 1–19 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan without any disagreement, and it is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Durays, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuaym in al-Hilyah related from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that he said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ is the first surah to be sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi (who graded it sahih) related from ʿAʾishah that she said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾. What indicates that this surah was the first to be revealed is the long, established hadith in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, in which it says: "The truth came to him while he was in the cave of Hira, and he said to him: Read..." – the hadith continues. On this topic there are other hadiths and reports from a group of the Companions.

The majority have held that this surah is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The majority read iqraʾ (اقْرَأْ) with a sukun on the hamzah, as an imperative from qiraʾah (recitation/reading).

ʿAsim, in one narration from him, read it with a fatha on the rāʾ (اقْرَأَ). It seems he converted the hamzah into an alif and then dropped it for the imperative. The command to recite requires something to be recited, so the implied meaning is: "Read what is revealed to you," or "what has been sent down to you," or "what you have been commanded to recite." The phrase bi-smi Rabbika (بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause: i.e., "Read while being associated with the name of your Lord," or "beginning with the name of your Lord," or "opening with the name of your Lord." It is also permissible for the bāʾ (ب) to be extra (زَائِدَة), so the meaning would be: "Read the name of your Lord," like the saying of the poet:

*Black-eyed (lit. "black sockets") ones who do not recite surahs*

Abu ʿUbaydah said this. He also said: the word ism (اسْم) is a supplement, i.e., "Remember your Lord."

It has been said that the bāʾ means "upon" (عَلَى): i.e., "Read upon the name of your Lord," as one says: "Do such-and-such in the name of Allah" and "upon the name of Allah." This was said by al-Akhfash.

It has been said that the bāʾ indicates seeking help: i.e., seeking help by the name of your Lord. He described the Lord with the words "who created" to remind of the blessing, because creation is the greatest of blessings, and all other blessings follow from it.

al-Kalbi said: He means the creatures.

﴿He created man from a clinging clot﴾ meaning the children of Adam. ʿAlaqah (عَلَقَة) is congealed blood; when it flows, it is called masfuh (مَسْفُوح, "poured forth").

He said: "from a clinging clot" (مِن عَلَقٍ) in the plural form ʿalaq, because the intended meaning of "man" is the species; the sense is: He created the species of man from the species of clot. If the intended meaning of "who created" is all created beings, then singling out man for mention is an honour for him, because of the wondrous creation and marvellous craftsmanship in him. If the intended meaning of "who created" is "who created man," then the second is an explanation of the first.

The subtle point lies in the ambiguity, then the explanation comes as the mind turns and looks forward to knowing what was first left vague and then explained second.

﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ i.e., do what you have been commanded of recitation. The clause "and your Lord is the Most Generous" is an independent clause to remove what the Prophet (ﷺ) had offered as an excuse when he said: "I am not a reader" (مَا أَنَا بِقَارِئٍ), meaning that reading is the matter of one who writes and reads, while he was unlettered. So it was said to him: "Read; and your Lord, who commanded you to read, is the Most Generous."

al-Kalbi said: He means the Forbearing toward the ignorance of His servants, so He did not hasten their punishment. It has also been said that He commanded him first to recite for himself, then commanded him again to recite for conveying the message, so it is not a case of emphasis; the first view is preferable.

﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ i.e., He taught man writing by the pen, so that by means of it he is able to know every written thing. al-Zajjaj said: He taught man writing by the pen.

Qatadah said: The pen is a great blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; were it not for it, religion would not be established and life would not be set right. Thus He showed the perfection of His generosity by teaching His servants what they did not know, and bringing them from the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge. He drew attention to the excellence of the science of writing because of its great benefits, which none encompasses except Him. Sciences were not recorded, wisdom was not fixed, the reports and sayings of the ancients were not preserved, and the revealed books of Allah were not preserved except by writing; were it not for it, the affairs of religion would not be upright, nor the affairs of this world. al-Raghib said: al-safʿ is taking hold of the forelock of a horse, i.e., the blackness of its forelock; and by consideration of the blackness it is said: "a mark of anger" (سَفْعَةُ غَضَبٍ), based on the smoky colour that rises on the face of one whose anger has intensified. It is said of the falcon "asfaʿ" because of the gleam of blackness in it, and a woman is "safʿaʾ" in colour. End of quote. It has also been said that it is derived from the scorching of fire and sun, when they change the face to blackness, and from this is the poet's saying:

*Blackened hearthstones in the resting-place of a cauldron*

His words "forelock" (نَاصِيَةٌ) is a substitute (badal) from "the forelock" (النَّاصِيَة). He substituted the indefinite for the definite because it is qualified by His words "lying, sinning." This is according to the school of the Kufans, for they do not permit substituting an indefinite noun for a definite noun except on condition that it is qualified.

As for the school of the Basrans, it is permissible to substitute an indefinite noun for a definite noun without condition, and they cited:

*"No, by your father, one better than you... the neighing and the snorting trouble me."*

The majority read ﴿ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾ in the genitive, and the correct reading is what we have mentioned.

al-Kisa'i, in one narration from him, read it in the nominative, by supposing an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a forelock." Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAbalah, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the accusative, as a dispraise.

Muqatil said: He informed about him that he is wicked and sinful, so He said "a forelock, lying, sinning," its interpretation being: its owner is a liar and a sinner.

﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ i.e., the people of his assembly. The nadi (نَادِي) is the gathering place where a people sit and gather, from relatives and clan; the meaning is: let him call his clan and his family so that they may help and support him. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And the assembly has been abused after you, O Kulayb"*

i.e., its people.

It has been said that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you threaten me, when I am the most numerous in assembly in the valley?" So there was revealed: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell﴾, i.e., the angels, the harsh and mighty ones. Thus said al-Zajjaj. al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: their singular is zabin. Abu ʿUbaydah said: zibniyah. It has been said: zabani. It has also been said that it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like ʿabadid and ababil.

Qatadah said: They are the police (al-shurtah) in the language of the Arabs, and the root of zabn is pushing away. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And one who is amazed at what he sees of our groaning; even if war had pushed him, he would not have been dismayed."*

The Arabs apply this name to one whose strength in seizing is intense. From it is the poet's saying:

Poetry: *"Generous with food at the far end (of the camp), generous in war, they are the Zabaniyya, mighty and dominant, great of wisdom."*

Then he repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿No! Do not obey him.﴾ That is, do not obey him in what he calls you to, namely abandoning the prayer. ﴿And prostrate yourself﴾: that is, pray to God without concern for him and without heeding his prohibition. ﴿And draw near﴾: that is, draw near to Him, glory be to Him, through obedience and worship.

It was also said that the meaning is: when you prostrate yourself, draw near to God through supplication.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Prostrate yourself, you, O Muhammad, and draw near, you, O Abu Jahl, to the Fire." But the first interpretation is the better one.

As for this prostration, the apparent meaning is that it refers to prayer. It was also said that it refers to the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed on reciting a verse of prostration). This is supported by what is established from the Prophet ﷺ regarding prostrating when reciting this verse, as will come, God willing.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* related from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, who said: "Jibril came to Muhammad ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril embraced him and then said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾, until he reached: ﴿what he did not know﴾."

In the two *Sahihs* and others, from the hadith of Aisha: "The angel came to him and said: 'Recite!' He said: 'I said: I am not a reciter.' He said: 'He seized me and pressed me until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a second time until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a third time until I reached exhaustion, and then said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance, recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen﴾," and the verse (continued).

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'If I see Muhammad praying at the Ka'bah, I will surely trample his neck.' This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'If he did, the angels would have seized him openly.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "The Prophet ﷺ was praying when Abu Jahl came and said: 'Did I not forbid you from this? You know that there is no man in this valley with more supporters than I.' So God revealed: ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾, ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾. The Prophet ﷺ then came while praying, and it was said to him: 'What prevents you?' He said: 'The space between me and him has become black.'"

Ibn Abbas said: "By God, had he moved, the angels would have seized him while the people were looking at him."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'Does Muhammad rub his face in the dirt among you?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By al-Lat and al-Uzza, if I see him praying like that, I will surely step on his neck and rub his face in the dirt.' He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was praying, intending to step on his neck. But what they saw was that he was backing away on his heels and shielding himself with his hand. He was asked: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Between me and him is a trench of fire, a terror, and wings.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb.'" He said: "God revealed: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ to the end of the surah." That is, Abu Jahl. ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾: that is, his people. ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾: that is, the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids, a servant when he prays?﴾ (p-1641) He said: "Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, when he threw the entrails (sala) on the back of the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was prostrating to God, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding His words: ﴿we will surely seize﴾ (lanasfa'an), that it means: "we will surely take hold of."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾ that it means: "his helpers."

We have already mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ used to prostrate in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and in ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 96, verse 1–19 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan without any disagreement, and it is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Durays, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuaym in al-Hilyah related from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that he said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ is the first surah to be sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi (who graded it sahih) related from ʿAʾishah that she said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾. What indicates that this surah was the first to be revealed is the long, established hadith in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, in which it says: "The truth came to him while he was in the cave of Hira, and he said to him: Read..." – the hadith continues. On this topic there are other hadiths and reports from a group of the Companions.

The majority have held that this surah is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The majority read iqraʾ (اقْرَأْ) with a sukun on the hamzah, as an imperative from qiraʾah (recitation/reading).

ʿAsim, in one narration from him, read it with a fatha on the rāʾ (اقْرَأَ). It seems he converted the hamzah into an alif and then dropped it for the imperative. The command to recite requires something to be recited, so the implied meaning is: "Read what is revealed to you," or "what has been sent down to you," or "what you have been commanded to recite." The phrase bi-smi Rabbika (بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause: i.e., "Read while being associated with the name of your Lord," or "beginning with the name of your Lord," or "opening with the name of your Lord." It is also permissible for the bāʾ (ب) to be extra (زَائِدَة), so the meaning would be: "Read the name of your Lord," like the saying of the poet:

*Black-eyed (lit. "black sockets") ones who do not recite surahs*

Abu ʿUbaydah said this. He also said: the word ism (اسْم) is a supplement, i.e., "Remember your Lord."

It has been said that the bāʾ means "upon" (عَلَى): i.e., "Read upon the name of your Lord," as one says: "Do such-and-such in the name of Allah" and "upon the name of Allah." This was said by al-Akhfash.

It has been said that the bāʾ indicates seeking help: i.e., seeking help by the name of your Lord. He described the Lord with the words "who created" to remind of the blessing, because creation is the greatest of blessings, and all other blessings follow from it.

al-Kalbi said: He means the creatures.

﴿He created man from a clinging clot﴾ meaning the children of Adam. ʿAlaqah (عَلَقَة) is congealed blood; when it flows, it is called masfuh (مَسْفُوح, "poured forth").

He said: "from a clinging clot" (مِن عَلَقٍ) in the plural form ʿalaq, because the intended meaning of "man" is the species; the sense is: He created the species of man from the species of clot. If the intended meaning of "who created" is all created beings, then singling out man for mention is an honour for him, because of the wondrous creation and marvellous craftsmanship in him. If the intended meaning of "who created" is "who created man," then the second is an explanation of the first.

The subtle point lies in the ambiguity, then the explanation comes as the mind turns and looks forward to knowing what was first left vague and then explained second.

﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ i.e., do what you have been commanded of recitation. The clause "and your Lord is the Most Generous" is an independent clause to remove what the Prophet (ﷺ) had offered as an excuse when he said: "I am not a reader" (مَا أَنَا بِقَارِئٍ), meaning that reading is the matter of one who writes and reads, while he was unlettered. So it was said to him: "Read; and your Lord, who commanded you to read, is the Most Generous."

al-Kalbi said: He means the Forbearing toward the ignorance of His servants, so He did not hasten their punishment. It has also been said that He commanded him first to recite for himself, then commanded him again to recite for conveying the message, so it is not a case of emphasis; the first view is preferable.

﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ i.e., He taught man writing by the pen, so that by means of it he is able to know every written thing. al-Zajjaj said: He taught man writing by the pen.

Qatadah said: The pen is a great blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; were it not for it, religion would not be established and life would not be set right. Thus He showed the perfection of His generosity by teaching His servants what they did not know, and bringing them from the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge. He drew attention to the excellence of the science of writing because of its great benefits, which none encompasses except Him. Sciences were not recorded, wisdom was not fixed, the reports and sayings of the ancients were not preserved, and the revealed books of Allah were not preserved except by writing; were it not for it, the affairs of religion would not be upright, nor the affairs of this world. It is called qalam (قَلَم, "pen") because it is trimmed (يُقَلَّم), i.e., cut.

﴿Taught man what he did not know﴾ This clause is a badal al-ishtimal (بَدَلُ اشْتِمَالٍ, an inclusive substitution) of the one before it: i.e., He taught him by means of the pen, from general and particular matters, what he did not know of them. It has been said that "man" here refers to Adam, as in His words: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. It has also been said that "man" here refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The preferable view is to take "man" in its general sense, and the meaning is: whoever among this species Allah taught by means of the pen, He has taught him what he did not know.

His words "Nay" (كَلَّا) are a rebuke and a deterrence for one who disbelieves the blessings of Allah upon him because of his transgression, even though no mention has preceded it. The meaning of ﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾ is that he exceeds the limit and is arrogant toward his Lord.

It has been said that "man" here refers to Abu Jahl, and that this is the meaning of this and what follows to the end of the surah, and that the revelation of this and what follows came later than the five verses mentioned at the beginning of this surah.

It has been said that "kalla" here means "truly" (حَقًّا); this was said by al-Jurjani, who justified it by saying that there is nothing before it or after it that would make "kalla" a refutation of it.

His words ﴿that he sees himself as self-sufficient﴾ are the cause for "transgresses": i.e., he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient, or because he sees himself as self-sufficient. The verb "sees" (رَأَى) here means "knows" (بِمَعْنَى العِلْم); if it were the sight of the eye, it would be impossible to join the two pronouns in its verb for one thing, because that is a characteristic of the class of ʿalima and similar verbs.

al-Farra' said: He did not say "he saw himself," as one says "he killed himself," because ra'a (رَأَى) is among the verbs that take a subject and a predicate, like "thought" and "reckoned," and so it is not restricted to one object; the Arabs drop the nafs in this class, saying: "I saw myself" (رَأَيْتُنِي), "I reckoned myself" (حَسِبْتُنِي), "when do you see yourself outside?" (مَتَى تَرَاكَ خَارِجًا), "when do you think you outside?" (مَتَى تَظُنُّكَ خَارِجًا). It has been said that the meaning here is that he deemed himself self-sufficient through his clan, his helpers, and his wealth.

al-Jumhur read ﴿أَنْ رَآهُ﴾ with a long alif (مَدّ الهَمْزَة).

Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a short vowel (قَصْرِها).

Muqatil said: When Abu Jahl acquired wealth, he increased his clothing, his mount, his food and his drink; that is his transgression. al-Kalbi said likewise.

Then He threatened and warned, saying: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ i.e., the destination. The words rujʿa (رُجْعَى), marji (مَرْجِع) and ruju' (رُجُوع) are verbal nouns: one says "he returned to him" (رَجَعَ إلَيْهِ) as marji', ruju' and ruj'a. The prepositional phrase has been placed first for restriction: i.e., the return is to Him, glorified is He, and not to anyone else.

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays?﴾ The exegetes said: "The one who forbids" is Abu Jahl, and "the servant" is Muhammad (ﷺ). This includes denunciation of his action and condemnation of his deed, as if he were in a position where everyone who is able to see it would see it.

﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance﴾ meaning the forbidden servant when he prays, who is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Or enjoins piety?﴾ i.e., enjoins sincerity, monotheism and righteous deeds by which one is protected from the Fire.

﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away?﴾ meaning Abu Jahl, who denied what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought and turned away from faith. His words "Have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) in the three places mean "inform me," because sight, being a cause of informing about the seen, makes the question about it take the place of a question about its object. The address is to everyone who is fit for it.

Here "Have you seen" is mentioned three times, and after the third one a question clause is stated explicitly, so it occupies the position of the second object of it. Its first object is omitted, which is a pronoun referring to "the one who forbids," which functions as the first object of the first "Have you seen." The second object of the first "Have you seen" is omitted, and it is a question clause like the clause after the second "Have you seen." As for the second "Have you seen," no object is mentioned for it, neither first nor second: the first has been omitted for the indication of the object of the third "Have you seen," so the second has been omitted from the first, the first from the third, and both from the second. The demand of each "Have you seen" for the question clause is not by way of tanazu' (competition between verbs), because that would require a pronominal supplement, and clauses are not supplied; only individual words are supplied. Rather, it is an omission for indication. As for the answer of the conditional clause mentioned with "Have you seen" in the two other places, it is omitted; its assumed form is: "if he is upon guidance, or enjoins piety."

﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ This is omitted here because its mention is an indication in the answer of the second conditional. The meaning of ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ is: He observes his conditions and will recompense him for them; so how has he dared to do what he has dared? The interrogation is for reproach and rebuke. It has been said: The first "Have you seen" has as its first object the relative pronoun, and its second object the first conditional clause with its omitted answer, indicated by what is mentioned; and the "Have you seen" in the two places is repetition for emphasis. It has also been said that each "Have you seen" is a substitute (badal) for the first, and "Does he not know that Allah sees?" is the predicate.

"Nay" (كَلَّا) is a deterrence for the forbidder. The lam in His words ﴿Surely if he does not desist﴾ is the lam that prepares for an oath: i.e., by Allah, if he does not desist from what he is upon and is not restrained, ﴿we will certainly seize him by the forelock﴾. Al-safʿ (السَّفْع) is a strong pulling. The meaning: we will certainly take hold of his forelock and drag him into the Fire. This is like His words: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. One says "I seized the thing" (سَفَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ) when you grasp and pull it, and "he seized the forelock of his horse" (سَفَعَ بِنَاصِيَةِ فَرَسِهِ).

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'Does Muhammad rub his face in the dirt among you?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By al-Lat and al-Uzza, if I see him praying like that, I will surely step on his neck and rub his face in the dirt.' He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was praying, intending to step on his neck. But what they saw was that he was backing away on his heels and shielding himself with his hand. He was asked: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Between me and him is a trench of fire, a terror, and wings.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb.'" He said: "God revealed: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ to the end of the surah." That is, Abu Jahl. ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾: that is, his people. ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾: that is, the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids, a servant when he prays?﴾ (p-1641) He said: "Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, when he threw the entrails (sala) on the back of the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was prostrating to God, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding His words: ﴿we will surely seize﴾ (lanasfa'an), that it means: "we will surely take hold of."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾ that it means: "his helpers."

We have already mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ used to prostrate in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and in ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

It is Meccan without any disagreement, and it is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Durays, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuaym in al-Hilyah related from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that he said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ is the first surah to be sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi (who graded it sahih) related from ʿAʾishah that she said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾. What indicates that this surah was the first to be revealed is the long, established hadith in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, in which it says: "The truth came to him while he was in the cave of Hira, and he said to him: Read..." – the hadith continues. On this topic there are other hadiths and reports from a group of the Companions.

The majority have held that this surah is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The majority read iqraʾ (اقْرَأْ) with a sukun on the hamzah, as an imperative from qiraʾah (recitation/reading).

ʿAsim, in one narration from him, read it with a fatha on the rāʾ (اقْرَأَ). It seems he converted the hamzah into an alif and then dropped it for the imperative. The command to recite requires something to be recited, so the implied meaning is: "Read what is revealed to you," or "what has been sent down to you," or "what you have been commanded to recite." The phrase bi-smi Rabbika (بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause: i.e., "Read while being associated with the name of your Lord," or "beginning with the name of your Lord," or "opening with the name of your Lord." It is also permissible for the bāʾ (ب) to be extra (زَائِدَة), so the meaning would be: "Read the name of your Lord," like the saying of the poet:

*Black-eyed (lit. "black sockets") ones who do not recite surahs*

Abu ʿUbaydah said this. He also said: the word ism (اسْم) is a supplement, i.e., "Remember your Lord."

It has been said that the bāʾ means "upon" (عَلَى): i.e., "Read upon the name of your Lord," as one says: "Do such-and-such in the name of Allah" and "upon the name of Allah." This was said by al-Akhfash.

It has been said that the bāʾ indicates seeking help: i.e., seeking help by the name of your Lord. He described the Lord with the words "who created" to remind of the blessing, because creation is the greatest of blessings, and all other blessings follow from it.

al-Kalbi said: He means the creatures.

﴿He created man from a clinging clot﴾ meaning the children of Adam. ʿAlaqah (عَلَقَة) is congealed blood; when it flows, it is called masfuh (مَسْفُوح, "poured forth").

He said: "from a clinging clot" (مِن عَلَقٍ) in the plural form ʿalaq, because the intended meaning of "man" is the species; the sense is: He created the species of man from the species of clot. If the intended meaning of "who created" is all created beings, then singling out man for mention is an honour for him, because of the wondrous creation and marvellous craftsmanship in him. If the intended meaning of "who created" is "who created man," then the second is an explanation of the first.

The subtle point lies in the ambiguity, then the explanation comes as the mind turns and looks forward to knowing what was first left vague and then explained second.

﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ i.e., do what you have been commanded of recitation. The clause "and your Lord is the Most Generous" is an independent clause to remove what the Prophet (ﷺ) had offered as an excuse when he said: "I am not a reader" (مَا أَنَا بِقَارِئٍ), meaning that reading is the matter of one who writes and reads, while he was unlettered. So it was said to him: "Read; and your Lord, who commanded you to read, is the Most Generous."

al-Kalbi said: He means the Forbearing toward the ignorance of His servants, so He did not hasten their punishment. It has also been said that He commanded him first to recite for himself, then commanded him again to recite for conveying the message, so it is not a case of emphasis; the first view is preferable.

﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ i.e., He taught man writing by the pen, so that by means of it he is able to know every written thing. al-Zajjaj said: He taught man writing by the pen.

Qatadah said: The pen is a great blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; were it not for it, religion would not be established and life would not be set right. Thus He showed the perfection of His generosity by teaching His servants what they did not know, and bringing them from the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge. He drew attention to the excellence of the science of writing because of its great benefits, which none encompasses except Him. Sciences were not recorded, wisdom was not fixed, the reports and sayings of the ancients were not preserved, and the revealed books of Allah were not preserved except by writing; were it not for it, the affairs of religion would not be upright, nor the affairs of this world. It is called qalam (قَلَم, "pen") because it is trimmed (يُقَلَّم), i.e., cut.

﴿Taught man what he did not know﴾ This clause is a badal al-ishtimal (بَدَلُ اشْتِمَالٍ, an inclusive substitution) of the one before it: i.e., He taught him by means of the pen, from general and particular matters, what he did not know of them. It has been said that "man" here refers to Adam, as in His words: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. It has also been said that "man" here refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The preferable view is to take "man" in its general sense, and the meaning is: whoever among this species Allah taught by means of the pen, He has taught him what he did not know.

His words "Nay" (كَلَّا) are a rebuke and a deterrence for one who disbelieves the blessings of Allah upon him because of his transgression, even though no mention has preceded it. The meaning of ﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾ is that he exceeds the limit and is arrogant toward his Lord.

It has been said that "man" here refers to Abu Jahl, and that this is the meaning of this and what follows to the end of the surah, and that the revelation of this and what follows came later than the five verses mentioned at the beginning of this surah.

It has been said that "kalla" here means "truly" (حَقًّا); this was said by al-Jurjani, who justified it by saying that there is nothing before it or after it that would make "kalla" a refutation of it.

His words ﴿that he sees himself as self-sufficient﴾ are the cause for "transgresses": i.e., he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient, or because he sees himself as self-sufficient. The verb "sees" (رَأَى) here means "knows" (بِمَعْنَى العِلْم); if it were the sight of the eye, it would be impossible to join the two pronouns in its verb for one thing, because that is a characteristic of the class of ʿalima and similar verbs.

al-Farra' said: He did not say "he saw himself," as one says "he killed himself," because ra'a (رَأَى) is among the verbs that take a subject and a predicate, like "thought" and "reckoned," and so it is not restricted to one object; the Arabs drop the nafs in this class, saying: "I saw myself" (رَأَيْتُنِي), "I reckoned myself" (حَسِبْتُنِي), "when do you see yourself outside?" (مَتَى تَرَاكَ خَارِجًا), "when do you think you outside?" (مَتَى تَظُنُّكَ خَارِجًا). It has been said that the meaning here is that he deemed himself self-sufficient through his clan, his helpers, and his wealth.

al-Jumhur read ﴿أَنْ رَآهُ﴾ with a long alif (مَدّ الهَمْزَة).

Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a short vowel (قَصْرِها).

Muqatil said: When Abu Jahl acquired wealth, he increased his clothing, his mount, his food and his drink; that is his transgression. al-Kalbi said likewise.

Then He threatened and warned, saying: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ i.e., the destination. The words rujʿa (رُجْعَى), marji (مَرْجِع) and ruju' (رُجُوع) are verbal nouns: one says "he returned to him" (رَجَعَ إلَيْهِ) as marji', ruju' and ruj'a. The prepositional phrase has been placed first for restriction: i.e., the return is to Him, glorified is He, and not to anyone else.

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays?﴾ The exegetes said: "The one who forbids" is Abu Jahl, and "the servant" is Muhammad (ﷺ). This includes denunciation of his action and condemnation of his deed, as if he were in a position where everyone who is able to see it would see it.

﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance﴾ meaning the forbidden servant when he prays, who is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Or enjoins piety?﴾ i.e., enjoins sincerity, monotheism and righteous deeds by which one is protected from the Fire.

﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away?﴾ meaning Abu Jahl, who denied what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought and turned away from faith. His words "Have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) in the three places mean "inform me," because sight, being a cause of informing about the seen, makes the question about it take the place of a question about its object. The address is to everyone who is fit for it.

Here "Have you seen" is mentioned three times, and after the third one a question clause is stated explicitly, so it occupies the position of the second object of it. Its first object is omitted, which is a pronoun referring to "the one who forbids," which functions as the first object of the first "Have you seen." The second object of the first "Have you seen" is omitted, and it is a question clause like the clause after the second "Have you seen." As for the second "Have you seen," no object is mentioned for it, neither first nor second: the first has been omitted for the indication of the object of the third "Have you seen," so the second has been omitted from the first, the first from the third, and both from the second. The demand of each "Have you seen" for the question clause is not by way of tanazu' (competition between verbs), because that would require a pronominal supplement, and clauses are not supplied; only individual words are supplied. Rather, it is an omission for indication. As for the answer of the conditional clause mentioned with "Have you seen" in the two other places, it is omitted; its assumed form is: "if he is upon guidance, or enjoins piety."

﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ This is omitted here because its mention is an indication in the answer of the second conditional. The meaning of ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ is: He observes his conditions and will recompense him for them; so how has he dared to do what he has dared? The interrogation is for reproach and rebuke. It has been said: The first "Have you seen" has as its first object the relative pronoun, and its second object the first conditional clause with its omitted answer, indicated by what is mentioned; and the "Have you seen" in the two places is repetition for emphasis. It has also been said that each "Have you seen" is a substitute (badal) for the first, and "Does he not know that Allah sees?" is the predicate.

"Nay" (كَلَّا) is a deterrence for the forbidder. The lam in His words ﴿Surely if he does not desist﴾ is the lam that prepares for an oath: i.e., by Allah, if he does not desist from what he is upon and is not restrained, ﴿we will certainly seize him by the forelock﴾. Al-safʿ (السَّفْع) is a strong pulling. The meaning: we will certainly take hold of his forelock and drag him into the Fire. This is like His words: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. One says "I seized the thing" (سَفَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ) when you grasp and pull it, and "he seized the forelock of his horse" (سَفَعَ بِنَاصِيَةِ فَرَسِهِ).

al-Raghib said: al-safʿ is taking hold of the forelock of a horse, i.e., the blackness of its forelock; and by consideration of the blackness it is said: "a mark of anger" (سَفْعَةُ غَضَبٍ), based on the smoky colour that rises on the face of one whose anger has intensified. It is said of the falcon "asfaʿ" because of the gleam of blackness in it, and a woman is "safʿaʾ" in colour. End of quote. It has also been said that it is derived from the scorching of fire and sun, when they change the face to blackness, and from this is the poet's saying:

*Blackened hearthstones in the resting-place of a cauldron*

His words "forelock" (نَاصِيَةٌ) is a substitute (badal) from "the forelock" (النَّاصِيَة). He substituted the indefinite for the definite because it is qualified by His words "lying, sinning." This is according to the school of the Kufans, for they do not permit substituting an indefinite noun for a definite noun except on condition that it is qualified.

As for the school of the Basrans, it is permissible to substitute an indefinite noun for a definite noun without condition, and they cited:

*"No, by your father, one better than you... the neighing and the snorting trouble me."*

The majority read ﴿ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾ in the genitive, and the correct reading is what we have mentioned.

al-Kisa'i, in one narration from him, read it in the nominative, by supposing an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a forelock." Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAbalah, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the accusative, as a dispraise.

Muqatil said: He informed about him that he is wicked and sinful, so He said "a forelock, lying, sinning," its interpretation being: its owner is a liar and a sinner.

﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ i.e., the people of his assembly. The nadi (نَادِي) is the gathering place where a people sit and gather, from relatives and clan; the meaning is: let him call his clan and his family so that they may help and support him. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And the assembly has been abused after you, O Kulayb"*

i.e., its people.

It has been said that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you threaten me, when I am the most numerous in assembly in the valley?" So there was revealed: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell﴾, i.e., the angels, the harsh and mighty ones. Thus said al-Zajjaj. al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: their singular is zabin. Abu ʿUbaydah said: zibniyah. It has been said: zabani. It has also been said that it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like ʿabadid and ababil.

Qatadah said: They are the police (al-shurtah) in the language of the Arabs, and the root of zabn is pushing away. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And one who is amazed at what he sees of our groaning; even if war had pushed him, he would not have been dismayed."*

The Arabs apply this name to one whose strength in seizing is intense. From it is the poet's saying:

Poetry: *"Generous with food at the far end (of the camp), generous in war, they are the Zabaniyya, mighty and dominant, great of wisdom."*

Then he repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿No! Do not obey him.﴾ That is, do not obey him in what he calls you to, namely abandoning the prayer. ﴿And prostrate yourself﴾: that is, pray to God without concern for him and without heeding his prohibition. ﴿And draw near﴾: that is, draw near to Him, glory be to Him, through obedience and worship.

It was also said that the meaning is: when you prostrate yourself, draw near to God through supplication.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Prostrate yourself, you, O Muhammad, and draw near, you, O Abu Jahl, to the Fire." But the first interpretation is the better one.

As for this prostration, the apparent meaning is that it refers to prayer. It was also said that it refers to the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed on reciting a verse of prostration). This is supported by what is established from the Prophet ﷺ regarding prostrating when reciting this verse, as will come, God willing.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* related from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, who said: "Jibril came to Muhammad ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril embraced him and then said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾, until he reached: ﴿what he did not know﴾."

In the two *Sahihs* and others, from the hadith of Aisha: "The angel came to him and said: 'Recite!' He said: 'I said: I am not a reciter.' He said: 'He seized me and pressed me until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a second time until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a third time until I reached exhaustion, and then said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance, recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen﴾," and the verse (continued).

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'If I see Muhammad praying at the Ka'bah, I will surely trample his neck.' This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'If he did, the angels would have seized him openly.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "The Prophet ﷺ was praying when Abu Jahl came and said: 'Did I not forbid you from this? You know that there is no man in this valley with more supporters than I.' So God revealed: ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾, ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾. The Prophet ﷺ then came while praying, and it was said to him: 'What prevents you?' He said: 'The space between me and him has become black.'"

Ibn Abbas said: "By God, had he moved, the angels would have seized him while the people were looking at him."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'Does Muhammad rub his face in the dirt among you?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By al-Lat and al-Uzza, if I see him praying like that, I will surely step on his neck and rub his face in the dirt.' He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was praying, intending to step on his neck. But what they saw was that he was backing away on his heels and shielding himself with his hand. He was asked: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Between me and him is a trench of fire, a terror, and wings.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb.'" He said: "God revealed: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ to the end of the surah." That is, Abu Jahl. ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾: that is, his people. ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾: that is, the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids, a servant when he prays?﴾ (p-1641) He said: "Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, when he threw the entrails (sala) on the back of the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was prostrating to God, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding His words: ﴿we will surely seize﴾ (lanasfa'an), that it means: "we will surely take hold of."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾ that it means: "his helpers."

We have already mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ used to prostrate in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and in ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Qatadah said: The pen is a great blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; were it not for it, religion would not be established and life would not be set right. Thus He showed the perfection of His generosity by teaching His servants what they did not know, and bringing them from the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge. He drew attention to the excellence of the science of writing because of its great benefits, which none encompasses except Him. Sciences were not recorded, wisdom was not fixed, the reports and sayings of the ancients were not preserved, and the revealed books of Allah were not preserved except by writing; were it not for it, the affairs of religion would not be upright, nor the affairs of this world. It is called qalam (قَلَم, "pen") because it is trimmed (يُقَلَّم), i.e., cut.

﴿Taught man what he did not know﴾ This clause is a badal al-ishtimal (بَدَلُ اشْتِمَالٍ, an inclusive substitution) of the one before it: i.e., He taught him by means of the pen, from general and particular matters, what he did not know of them. It has been said that "man" here refers to Adam, as in His words: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. It has also been said that "man" here refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The preferable view is to take "man" in its general sense, and the meaning is: whoever among this species Allah taught by means of the pen, He has taught him what he did not know.

His words "Nay" (كَلَّا) are a rebuke and a deterrence for one who disbelieves the blessings of Allah upon him because of his transgression, even though no mention has preceded it. The meaning of ﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾ is that he exceeds the limit and is arrogant toward his Lord.

It has been said that "man" here refers to Abu Jahl, and that this is the meaning of this and what follows to the end of the surah, and that the revelation of this and what follows came later than the five verses mentioned at the beginning of this surah.

It has been said that "kalla" here means "truly" (حَقًّا); this was said by al-Jurjani, who justified it by saying that there is nothing before it or after it that would make "kalla" a refutation of it.

His words ﴿that he sees himself as self-sufficient﴾ are the cause for "transgresses": i.e., he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient, or because he sees himself as self-sufficient. The verb "sees" (رَأَى) here means "knows" (بِمَعْنَى العِلْم); if it were the sight of the eye, it would be impossible to join the two pronouns in its verb for one thing, because that is a characteristic of the class of ʿalima and similar verbs.

al-Farra' said: He did not say "he saw himself," as one says "he killed himself," because ra'a (رَأَى) is among the verbs that take a subject and a predicate, like "thought" and "reckoned," and so it is not restricted to one object; the Arabs drop the nafs in this class, saying: "I saw myself" (رَأَيْتُنِي), "I reckoned myself" (حَسِبْتُنِي), "when do you see yourself outside?" (مَتَى تَرَاكَ خَارِجًا), "when do you think you outside?" (مَتَى تَظُنُّكَ خَارِجًا). It has been said that the meaning here is that he deemed himself self-sufficient through his clan, his helpers, and his wealth.

al-Jumhur read ﴿أَنْ رَآهُ﴾ with a long alif (مَدّ الهَمْزَة).

Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a short vowel (قَصْرِها).

Muqatil said: When Abu Jahl acquired wealth, he increased his clothing, his mount, his food and his drink; that is his transgression. al-Kalbi said likewise.

Then He threatened and warned, saying: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ i.e., the destination. The words rujʿa (رُجْعَى), marji (مَرْجِع) and ruju' (رُجُوع) are verbal nouns: one says "he returned to him" (رَجَعَ إلَيْهِ) as marji', ruju' and ruj'a. The prepositional phrase has been placed first for restriction: i.e., the return is to Him, glorified is He, and not to anyone else.

This includes denunciation of his action and condemnation of his deed, as if he were in a position where everyone who is able to see it would see it.

﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance﴾ meaning the forbidden servant when he prays, who is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Or enjoins piety?﴾ i.e., enjoins sincerity, monotheism and righteous deeds by which one is protected from the Fire.

His words "Have you seen" (أَرَأَيْتَ) in the three places mean "inform me," because sight, being a cause of informing about the seen, makes the question about it take the place of a question about its object. The address is to everyone who is fit for it.

Here "Have you seen" is mentioned three times, and after the third one a question clause is stated explicitly, so it occupies the position of the second object of it. Its first object is omitted, which is a pronoun referring to "the one who forbids," which functions as the first object of the first "Have you seen." The second object of the first "Have you seen" is omitted, and it is a question clause like the clause after the second "Have you seen." As for the second "Have you seen," no object is mentioned for it, neither first nor second: the first has been omitted for the indication of the object of the third "Have you seen," so the second has been omitted from the first, the first from the third, and both from the second. The demand of each "Have you seen" for the question clause is not by way of tanazu' (competition between verbs), because that would require a pronominal supplement, and clauses are not supplied; only individual words are supplied. Rather, it is an omission for indication. As for the answer of the conditional clause mentioned with "Have you seen" in the two other places, it is omitted; its assumed form is: "if he is upon guidance, or enjoins piety."

﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ This is omitted here because its mention is an indication in the answer of the second conditional. The meaning of ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ is: He observes his conditions and will recompense him for them; so how has he dared to do what he has dared? The interrogation is for reproach and rebuke. It has been said: The first "Have you seen" has as its first object the relative pronoun, and its second object the first conditional clause with its omitted answer, indicated by what is mentioned; and the "Have you seen" in the two places is repetition for emphasis. It has also been said that each "Have you seen" is a substitute (badal) for the first, and "Does he not know that Allah sees?" is the predicate.

"Nay" (كَلَّا) is a deterrence for the forbidder. The lam in His words ﴿Surely if he does not desist﴾ is the lam that prepares for an oath: i.e., by Allah, if he does not desist from what he is upon and is not restrained, ﴿we will certainly seize him by the forelock﴾. Al-safʿ (السَّفْع) is a strong pulling. The meaning: we will certainly take hold of his forelock and drag him into the Fire. This is like His words: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. One says "I seized the thing" (سَفَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ) when you grasp and pull it, and "he seized the forelock of his horse" (سَفَعَ بِنَاصِيَةِ فَرَسِهِ).

al-Raghib said: al-safʿ is taking hold of the forelock of a horse, i.e., the blackness of its forelock; and by consideration of the blackness it is said: "a mark of anger" (سَفْعَةُ غَضَبٍ), based on the smoky colour that rises on the face of one whose anger has intensified. It is said of the falcon "asfaʿ" because of the gleam of blackness in it, and a woman is "safʿaʾ" in colour. End of quote. It has also been said that it is derived from the scorching of fire and sun, when they change the face to blackness, and from this is the poet's saying:

*Blackened hearthstones in the resting-place of a cauldron*

His words "forelock" (نَاصِيَةٌ) is a substitute (badal) from "the forelock" (النَّاصِيَة). He substituted the indefinite for the definite because it is qualified by His words "lying, sinning." This is according to the school of the Kufans, for they do not permit substituting an indefinite noun for a definite noun except on condition that it is qualified.

As for the school of the Basrans, it is permissible to substitute an indefinite noun for a definite noun without condition, and they cited:

*"No, by your father, one better than you... the neighing and the snorting trouble me."*

The majority read ﴿ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾ in the genitive, and the correct reading is what we have mentioned.

al-Kisa'i, in one narration from him, read it in the nominative, by supposing an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a forelock." Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAbalah, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the accusative, as a dispraise.

Muqatil said: He informed about him that he is wicked and sinful, so He said "a forelock, lying, sinning," its interpretation being: its owner is a liar and a sinner.

﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ i.e., the people of his assembly. The nadi (نَادِي) is the gathering place where a people sit and gather, from relatives and clan; the meaning is: let him call his clan and his family so that they may help and support him. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And the assembly has been abused after you, O Kulayb"*

i.e., its people.

It has been said that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you threaten me, when I am the most numerous in assembly in the valley?" So there was revealed: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell﴾, i.e., the angels, the harsh and mighty ones. Thus said al-Zajjaj. al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: their singular is zabin. Abu ʿUbaydah said: zibniyah. It has been said: zabani. It has also been said that it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like ʿabadid and ababil.

Qatadah said: They are the police (al-shurtah) in the language of the Arabs, and the root of zabn is pushing away. From it is the poet's saying:

*"And one who is amazed at what he sees of our groaning; even if war had pushed him, he would not have been dismayed."*

The Arabs apply this name to one whose strength in seizing is intense. From it is the poet's saying:

Poetry: *"Generous with food at the far end (of the camp), generous in war, they are the Zabaniyya, mighty and dominant, great of wisdom."*

Then he repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿No! Do not obey him.﴾ That is, do not obey him in what he calls you to, namely abandoning the prayer. ﴿And prostrate yourself﴾: that is, pray to God without concern for him and without heeding his prohibition. ﴿And draw near﴾: that is, draw near to Him, glory be to Him, through obedience and worship.

It was also said that the meaning is: when you prostrate yourself, draw near to God through supplication.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Prostrate yourself, you, O Muhammad, and draw near, you, O Abu Jahl, to the Fire." But the first interpretation is the better one.

As for this prostration, the apparent meaning is that it refers to prayer. It was also said that it refers to the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed on reciting a verse of prostration). This is supported by what is established from the Prophet ﷺ regarding prostrating when reciting this verse, as will come, God willing.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* related from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, who said: "Jibril came to Muhammad ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril embraced him and then said: 'O Muhammad, recite!' He said: 'What shall I recite?' Jibril said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾, until he reached: ﴿what he did not know﴾."

In the two *Sahihs* and others, from the hadith of Aisha: "The angel came to him and said: 'Recite!' He said: 'I said: I am not a reciter.' He said: 'He seized me and pressed me until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a second time until I reached exhaustion. Then he released me and said: Recite! I said: I am not a reciter. He pressed me a third time until I reached exhaustion, and then said: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance, recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen﴾," and the verse (continued).

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'If I see Muhammad praying at the Ka'bah, I will surely trample his neck.' This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'If he did, the angels would have seized him openly.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "The Prophet ﷺ was praying when Abu Jahl came and said: 'Did I not forbid you from this? You know that there is no man in this valley with more supporters than I.' So God revealed: ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾, ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾. The Prophet ﷺ then came while praying, and it was said to him: 'What prevents you?' He said: 'The space between me and him has become black.'"

Ibn Abbas said: "By God, had he moved, the angels would have seized him while the people were looking at him."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Abu Jahl said: 'Does Muhammad rub his face in the dirt among you?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By al-Lat and al-Uzza, if I see him praying like that, I will surely step on his neck and rub his face in the dirt.' He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was praying, intending to step on his neck. But what they saw was that he was backing away on his heels and shielding himself with his hand. He was asked: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Between me and him is a trench of fire, a terror, and wings.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb.'" He said: "God revealed: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ to the end of the surah." That is, Abu Jahl. ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾: that is, his people. ﴿We will call the Zabaniyya﴾: that is, the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids, a servant when he prays?﴾ (p-1641) He said: "Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, when he threw the entrails (sala) on the back of the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was prostrating to God, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding His words: ﴿we will surely seize﴾ (lanasfa'an), that it means: "we will surely take hold of."

Ibn Jarir related from him also regarding ﴿Then let him call his associates﴾ that it means: "his helpers."

We have already mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ used to prostrate in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and in ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 96, verse 1–19 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan without any disagreement, and it is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Durays, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuaym in al-Hilyah related from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that he said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ is the first surah to be sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi (who graded it sahih) related from ʿAʾishah that she said: The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾. What indicates that this surah was the first to be revealed is the long, established hadith in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, in which it says: "The truth came to him while he was in the cave of Hira, and he said to him: Read..." – the hadith continues. On this topic there are other hadiths and reports from a group of the Companions.

The majority have held that this surah is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The majority read iqraʾ (اقْرَأْ) with a sukun on the hamzah, as an imperative from qiraʾah (recitation/reading).

ʿAsim, in one narration from him, read it with a fatha on the rāʾ (اقْرَأَ). It seems he converted the hamzah into an alif and then dropped it for the imperative. The command to recite requires something to be recited, so the implied meaning is: "Read what is revealed to you," or "what has been sent down to you," or "what you have been commanded to recite." The phrase bi-smi Rabbika (بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause: i.e., "Read while being associated with the name of your Lord," or "beginning with the name of your Lord," or "opening with the name of your Lord." It is also permissible for the bāʾ (ب) to be extra (زَائِدَة), so the meaning would be: "Read the name of your Lord," like the saying of the poet:

*Black-eyed (lit. "black sockets") ones who do not recite surahs*

Abu ʿUbaydah said this. He also said: the word ism (اسْم) is a supplement, i.e., "Remember your Lord."

It has been said that the bāʾ means "upon" (عَلَى): i.e., "Read upon the name of your Lord," as one says: "Do such-and-such in the name of Allah" and "upon the name of Allah." This was said by al-Akhfash.

It has been said that the bāʾ indicates seeking help: i.e., seeking help by the name of your Lord. He described the Lord with the words "who created" to remind of the blessing, because creation is the greatest of blessings, and all other blessings follow from it.

al-Kalbi said: He means the creatures.

﴿He created man from a clinging clot﴾ meaning the children of Adam. ʿAlaqah (عَلَقَة) is congealed blood; when it flows, it is called masfuh (مَسْفُوح, "poured forth").

He said: "from a clinging clot" (مِن عَلَقٍ) in the plural form ʿalaq, because the intended meaning of "man" is the species; the sense is: He created the species of man from the species of clot. If the intended meaning of "who created" is all created beings, then singling out man for mention is an honour for him, because of the wondrous creation and marvellous craftsmanship in him. If the intended meaning of "who created" is "who created man," then the second is an explanation of the first.

The subtle point lies in the ambiguity, then the explanation comes as the mind turns and looks forward to knowing what was first left vague and then explained second.
